items.answer: Usability is an explicit measure of how good a system is from the point of view of the user: the extent to which a product can be used by specified users to achieve specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction in a specified context of use.

An extended reality system is an interactive system that comprises hardware, an XR engine as middleware, and the application layer, in which input devices track the user's actions and positions, send them as input data, the data is processed to render an environment, and output devices stimulate the user's senses.

Extended reality (XR) is an umbrella term, not a specific technology, that covers all present or future immersive technologies, such as augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR).

Augmented reality (AR) is an enhanced version of reality created by technology, in which computer-generated digital content is overlaid on the real world in real time and registered in 3D, so the user perceives and interacts with the enhanced environment.
Mixed reality (MR) is an immersive technology that is the same as augmented reality, in which digital content is overlaid on the view of reality and can be interacted with.

Immersion is the objective, quantifiable degree to which a virtual reality system projects stimuli onto the sensory receptors of users in an extensive, matching, surrounding, vivid, interactive, and plot-informing way.

questions.question: Which design aspect of an XR system is concerned with its output rather than its input?
options: Immersion design
Interaction design
Presence design
Perceptual design
questions.explanation: Perceptual design concerns output and makes it appropriately sensed, understood, or perceived by the user. Interaction design concerns input and ease of interacting, while presence is an outcome of the illusion rather than a separate output-design category.

questions.question: Why are XR interaction and perceptual stimuli designed as an illusion of reality rather than as actual reality?
options: To hide the user’s sense of presence
To replace the user’s sense of presence
To reduce the user’s sense of presence
To enhance the user’s sense of presence
questions.explanation: The illusion is created to enhance presence, the feeling of being in a real world. Reducing, replacing, or hiding presence would work against that purpose.

questions.question: What makes the illusion of reality more central in VR than in AR or MR?
options: VR aims for total immersion
AR aims for total immersion
VR aims for partial immersion
MR aims for total immersion
questions.explanation: VR targets total immersion in a virtual environment, so the illusion carries more weight. AR and MR provide partial immersion because the real world remains viewable or experienced.

data.text: An XR system needs both interaction design and perceptual design so users can interact with it and perceive its outputs. These interaction and perceptual elements aim to create the best possible illusion of reality, rather than actual reality, and thereby enhance presence. That illusion matters most in VR because VR seeks total immersion, while in AR or MR it is less significant, though not totally insignificant, because the real world remains viewable or experienced.
points: In XR, interaction design is about input, perceptual design is about output, and both support usability.
XR interaction and perceptual stimuli aim to create the best possible illusion of reality, not actual reality, to enhance presence.
The illusion of reality is crucial in VR, but less significant, not totally insignificant, in AR or MR.

questions.question: What must a VR system do for the user to feel strongly present?
options: Present sensory signals that are usually consistent with the user's real-life behavior
Keep the virtual environment visually simple so the brain can rest
Fool the user's perceptual system into accepting the virtual world as real
Reduce the user's awareness of the physical display hardware
questions.explanation: Presence in VR depends on making the user's perceptual system accept the virtual system as the familiar real world. Consistency with real-life behavior is not the basis of presence, because VR generally provides inconsistent signals.

questions.question: What can happen to a user's awareness of system flaws after successful adaptation to inconsistent VR stimulation?
options: The user may report the flaws to a developer
The user may see the flaws as harmless
The user may become unaware of the flaws
The user may become more aware of the flaws
questions.explanation: Successful adaptation to inconsistent VR stimulation can make the user unaware of flaws in the system. Noticing flaws more clearly or reporting them is not the adaptation outcome.

questions.question: What can happen when a user's body does not adapt to generally inconsistent VR stimulation?
options: The user may stop noticing flaws and may take the virtual system for the real world
The user may feel more relaxed and may become unaware of the display hardware
The user may feel increased fatigue or headaches, and may develop cyber sickness
The user may remember the virtual environment better and may report less presence
questions.explanation: When the body cannot adapt to inconsistent VR stimulation, the result can be increased fatigue or headaches, and this non-adaptation may lead to cyber sickness such as dizziness or nausea. Taking the virtual system for the real world is an effect of adaptation, not of non-adaptation.

questions.question: Why is knowledge of human perception needed for work on a VR system?
options: To improve the speed of user testing
To improve the appeal of an application domain
To improve the design of a VR system
To improve the accuracy of head tracking
questions.explanation: Understanding human perception helps make VR systems better by guiding design choices. It is not a method for improving tracking, market appeal, or testing speed.

data.text: VR aims to create presence by fooling the user's perceptual system into accepting the virtual world as real. Human perception is formed from evolved physiology and stored experience, while VR generally supplies sensory signals inconsistent with real-life experience and behavior. That inconsistency can lead either to adaptation, where the user accepts the virtual system as real, or to non-adaptation, which may cause cybersickness. These risks motivate studying human perception to design better VR systems and resolve flaws in existing ones.
points: VR creates presence by fooling perceptual mechanisms that evolved for the real world through artificial stimulation.
Human perception is formed from physiology and experience stored in long-term memory.
Virtual reality generally provides sensory signals inconsistent with the user's real-life experiences and behavior.
Inconsistent VR stimulation can lead to accepting the virtual as real or to non-adaptation, causing cybersickness.
Understanding human perception is needed to design better VR systems or identify and resolve flaws in them.

questions.question: What does perceptual psychology study?
options: How the brain converts sensory stimulation into perceived phenomena
How virtual displays convert digital stimulation into perceived phenomena
How the sensory organs convert real-world stimulation into perceived phenomena
How neural pathways convert sensory stimulation into perceived phenomena
questions.explanation: Perceptual psychology is the science of how the brain turns sensory stimulation received from the real world into perceived phenomena. The sensory organs and displays are not the subject of the conversion.

questions.question: Why is knowledge of perceptual psychology especially important for extended reality systems?
options: Because extended reality systems explicitly extend the user's deeply embedded idea of reality
Because extended reality systems deliberately copy the user's deeply embedded idea of reality
Because extended reality systems deliberately weaken the user's deeply embedded idea of reality
Because extended reality systems deliberately replace the user's deeply embedded idea of reality
questions.explanation: Extended reality systems are particularly important targets for perceptual psychology because their goal is to extend the user's deeply embedded idea of reality. Replacing, copying, or weakening that idea is not the stated reason.

questions.question: What does perceptual psychology provide to designers of extended reality systems?
options: Guidelines for judging how an XR system's price will be set
Guidelines for judging how an XR system's input will be controlled
Guidelines for judging how an XR system's content will be stored
Guidelines for judging how an XR system's output will be perceived
questions.explanation: Perceptual psychology helps by answering questions about how virtual output is perceived, such as apparent distance, visible pixels, motion smoothness, head height, sound location, fatigue, and presence. It is not primarily about input control, storage, or pricing.

questions.question: Which set of knowledge areas is needed for perceptual psychology in XR design?
options: Human physiology, experimental perceptual psychology, and XR interference with perception
Human physiology, experimental perceptual psychology, and XR marketing research
Human physiology, experimental perceptual psychology, and XR network latency
Human physiology, experimental perceptual psychology, and XR code optimization
questions.explanation: Perceptual psychology requires knowledge of the body's sense organs and neural pathways, of experimental perceptual psychology, and of how an engineered XR system interferes with normal perceptual processes. Marketing, network latency, and code optimization are not part of that required knowledge set.

data.text: Perceptual psychology studies how the brain turns sensory input into perceived phenomena. It matters especially for XR because XR explicitly extends the user's deeply embedded idea of reality. Perceptual psychology therefore frames XR design questions about hardware and user effects, and it requires knowledge of human physiology, theories from experimental perceptual psychology, and how engineered XR systems can interfere with common perceptual processes, with side effects such as nausea.
points: Perceptual psychology is the science of how the brain converts real-world sensory stimulation into perceived phenomena.
Knowledge of perceptual psychology is especially important for XR because XR explicitly extends the user's deeply embedded idea of reality.
Perceptual psychology guides better XR hardware design and understanding of user effects by answering design questions.
Perceptual psychology requires knowledge of human physiology, theories from experimental perceptual psychology, and XR interference with common perceptual processes.

questions.question: When speaking of the human body, what does a bodily sensor convert a stimulus into?
options: Air pressure waves
Electromagnetic energy
Neural impulses
Electrical signals
questions.explanation: In the human body, sensors convert stimuli into neural impulses; electrical signals are the device-sensor meaning, while air pressure waves and electromagnetic energy are stimuli for other senses.

questions.question: Which human sense is classified with both mechanoreceptors and thermoreceptors?
options: The auditory sense
The taste sense
The touch sense
The balance sense
questions.explanation: Touch is the sense that involves both mechanoreceptors and thermoreceptors; auditory and balance involve mechanoreceptors, while taste involves chemoreceptors.

questions.question: Which stimulus is paired with the balance sense?
options: Chemical composition of matter
Tissue distortion in skin and muscles
Electromagnetic energy in the visible range
Gravity or acceleration
questions.explanation: The balance sense is paired with gravity or acceleration. Electromagnetic energy in the visible range is paired with vision, tissue distortion in skin and muscles with touch, and chemical composition of matter with taste or smell.

data.text: The term sensor connects machine systems and the human body by separating device sensors from human bodily sensors. Stimulus, receptor, and sense organ form the common scheme for organizing the six human senses. This scheme marks balance as unusual, because it has no specific organ, even though vestibular organs act as sense organs for it.
points: A device sensor converts energy into electrical signals; a human bodily sensor converts stimuli into neural impulses.
Vision, auditory, touch, balance, taste, and smell are classified by stimulus, receptor, and sense organ.
Balance has no specific organ unlike the other five senses, though vestibular organs act as sense organs.

questions.question: What does selectivity in a sensory system describe?
options: An electrical signal being generated by a particular stimulus
A perception being formed by a particular stimulus
A neural impulse being propagated by a particular stimulus
A receptor being activated by a particular stimulus
questions.explanation: Sensory selectivity is about sense-organ receptors responding to a particular kind of stimulus, not about later interpretation, propagation, or device signal generation.

questions.question: Which stimulus activates the photoreceptors in the eye?
options: Temperature change in the skin-warmth range
Electromagnetic energy in the visible light range
Chemical composition in the odorant range
Mechanical vibration in the audible sound range
questions.explanation: Photoreceptors respond to electromagnetic energy at visible-light frequencies. The other options match auditory, thermal, and chemical sensing instead of vision.

questions.question: What do the additional receptors in touch detect?
options: Changes in tissue distortion
Changes in temperature
Changes in head orientation
Changes in air pressure
questions.explanation: The additional receptors in touch signal temperature change. Head orientation, tissue distortion, and air pressure belong to other senses or to the mechanoreceptor part of touch.

questions.question: What aspect of a stimulus do the taste and smell receptors signal?
options: motion of the skin
force of gravity
chemical composition of matter
frequency of visible light
questions.explanation: Taste and smell receptors report the chemical composition of matter, while light frequency, gravity, and skin motion belong to other senses.

data.text: Sensory system selectivity means that receptors in a sense organ respond only to a particular type of stimulus. Different senses are therefore built from different receptors: photoreceptors detect visible light, mechanoreceptors detect motion, vibration, or gravitational force, thermoreceptors detect temperature, and chemoreceptors detect chemical composition. This organizes the senses by the stimulus each receptor responds to.
points: Sensory system selectivity means sense-organ receptors target particular stimuli and activate only to a specific stimulus.
The eyes contain photoreceptors, which activate only to electromagnetic energy in the visible-light frequency range.
Auditory, touch, and balance use mechanoreceptors for motion, vibration, or gravitational force; touch adds thermoreceptors, balance: head and upward direction.
Taste and smell rely on chemoreceptors that signal based on chemical composition, in the tongue and nasal passage.

questions.question: What part of perceptual psychology deals with the body's sensing mechanisms?
options: the psychology of presence
the physiology of the senses
the perception of sensory signals
the study of user characteristics
questions.explanation: The physiology of the senses is the part of perceptual psychology concerned with the body's sensing mechanisms. Perception, presence, and user characteristics are related human-factor topics, but they are not the physiological part of perceptual psychology.

questions.question: For each of the six senses, what are receptors part of?
options: the perceptual process
the sensory stimuli
the sensory organs
the neural impulses
questions.explanation: For each sense, receptors are part of the sensory organ that receives the relevant stimuli. The perceptual process, stimuli, and neural impulses are related to sensing, but receptors are not part of them.

questions.question: In the human body, what are sensory organs considered to be?
options: the hardware of sensing
the perception of sensing
the output of sensing
the software of sensing
questions.explanation: Sensory organs are the hardware of sensing in the human body. The other options invert the hardware metaphor or confuse sensing with later perceptual or system output.

data.text: Perceptual psychology provides the needed background for human factors in XR systems, with sensory physiology as one of its parts. The six senses are considered, and each sense is linked to sensory organs whose receptors receive stimuli depending on the organ. Those sensory organs form the human body’s hardware of sensing, and their receptor types include photoreceptors, chemoreceptors, and mechanoreceptors.
points: Some knowledge of perceptual psychology, including sensory physiology, is needed to understand human factors in XR systems.
The six senses are vision, auditory, balance, taste, smell, and touch.
For each sense, receptors in its sensory organs receive stimuli depending on that sensory organ.
Different types of receptors include photoreceptors, chemoreceptors, and mechanoreceptors.
In the human body, sensory organs are the hardware of sensing.

Vibration
Gravity
Temperature
items.reason: Motion, vibration, and gravity are sensed by mechanoreceptors; temperature is detected by thermoreceptors.

questions.question: How do interaction design and perceptual design together support usability in an extended reality system?
questions.reference_answer: Interaction design supports usability by making the user's input easier to perform, while perceptual design supports it by making the system's output appropriately sensed and understood. Together they help specified users achieve their goals with effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction.

questions.question: How can generally inconsistent sensory stimulation in virtual reality lead to presence in one case and cybersickness in another?
questions.reference_answer: Virtual reality often supplies the brain with sensory signals that do not match real-life experience, and the body may either adapt or not. If it adapts, the user can stop noticing flaws and may believe the virtual system is real, supporting presence. If it does not adapt, the mismatch can cause fatigue, headaches, dizziness, nausea, or other cybersickness symptoms.

questions.question: Why is creating a convincing illusion of reality more crucial for virtual reality than for augmented or mixed reality?
questions.reference_answer: Virtual reality needs the illusion more because it aims for total immersion in a virtual environment, while augmented and mixed reality leave the real world available and are only partly immersive. XR interaction and output are designed to create such an illusion to enhance presence. Therefore, presence in virtual reality depends on fooling the perceptual system into accepting the virtual system as real.
